ai_features.name: rag_example_app
ai_features.tier_decision_rationale: The whole point of this example is to illustrate the use of RAG, so the retrieval pipeline is intentional despite the small dataset size.
ai_features.rough_description: Takes a natural-language question plus a small public dataset and produces a generated answer grounded in retrieved passages from that dataset, illustrating the RAG pattern end-to-end.
ai_features.purpose: Demonstrate the retrieval-augmented generation pattern end-to-end by answering a visitor's natural-language question with a generated response grounded in passages retrieved from a small public reference dataset.

invocation.trigger: A visitor opens the RAG example app from the landing page and submits a natural-language question

inputs.name: user_question
inputs.description: The natural-language question submitted by the visitor

inputs.name: reference_dataset
inputs.description: Small, fixed public dataset of documents/passages used as the retrieval corpus for this example

outputs.primary: A generated natural-language answer to the question, accompanied by the specific retrieved passages that grounded it, so a visitor can see the retrieval-to-answer chain
outputs.schema_notes: Object with fields: answer (string), retrieved_passages (array of {passage_id, source_title, text_excerpt, similarity_score}), and a short explanatory note pointing out which passage(s) informed which part of the answer

success_criteria: For questions covered by the dataset, at least the top retrieved passage is topically relevant to the question (measured via relevance labels or human spot-check)
The generated answer contains content traceable to the retrieved passages (e.g. paraphrase or quote overlap) rather than being generic or unrelated
A visitor with no prior knowledge of RAG can, from the displayed passages and answer together, understand that retrieval fed into generation
Answer generation completes and displays within budgeted latency for at least 95% of requests

failure_modes.mode: Retrieved passages are irrelevant to the question (dataset gap or poor embedding match)
failure_modes.mitigation: Show a similarity-score threshold; below threshold, display an explicit 'no strong match found in this dataset' message instead of forcing an answer

failure_modes.mode: Generated answer ignores retrieved passages and hallucinates instead
failure_modes.mitigation: Prompt template explicitly instructs the model to answer only from provided passages and to cite which passage supports each claim; validate citations reference passages actually retrieved

failure_modes.mode: Shared embedding or generation service is unavailable when a question is submitted
failure_modes.mitigation: Return a clear error state in the UI and log the outage; no silent fallback that fabricates an answer

failure_modes.mode: Question is out of scope for the small dataset entirely
failure_modes.mitigation: Explicitly state in the UI that the dataset is small and topic-limited; return a graceful 'not covered by this dataset' response rather than a low-confidence guess

ai_features.escalation: On retrieval or generation service failure, surface a user-facing error state (no answer generated) and log the incident for shared_framework_services monitoring; no automatic retry loop beyond a single transient-error retry.

eval_approach.offline: Curate a small set of question/expected-passage pairs from the reference dataset; verify retrieval returns the expected passage in top-k and that a held-out reviewer confirms the generated answer reflects the passage content
eval_approach.online: Log retrieval similarity scores, whether the answer text overlaps lexically/semantically with retrieved passages, and visitor-facing error rates; sample transcripts periodically for manual relevance and groundedness review
eval_approach.ground_truth: Manually authored question-to-passage mappings for the fixed dataset, created once during dataset curation and reused as a small regression eval set

privacy_safety: Reference dataset is public and non-sensitive by design; no user PII is stored beyond the transient question text needed to serve the response
User questions are not persisted beyond logging needed for debugging/eval, and are not linked to visitor identity
Generated answers are constrained to dataset content to avoid producing unrelated or unsafe open-domain claims

mechanisms.name: structured_outputs
mechanisms.rationale: Forcing the response into a schema with distinct answer and retrieved_passages fields makes the retrieval-to-generation link visible and inspectable, which is the whole educational point of the example

configuration.schema: { answer: string, retrieved_passages: [{passage_id, source_title, text_excerpt, similarity_score}] }

references: Lewis et al., 'Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks', https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401

knowledge_sources.name: example_public_dataset_embeddings
knowledge_sources.content_description: Embeddings of passages from a small, fixed, publicly licensed dataset (e.g. a curated set of short articles) used solely to illustrate retrieval for this example app

served_features.name: RAG_Example_App
served_features.purpose: Demonstrates the retrieval-augmented generation pattern in an educational way, letting a visitor see how a question is answered by combining a small public dataset with generated text.

invocation.trigger: A visitor opens the RAG example app from the landing page and submits a question.

inputs.name: user_question
inputs.description: The question the visitor wants answered using the example dataset.

inputs.name: reference_dataset
inputs.description: A small, publicly available set of documents used as the knowledge source for retrieval.

outputs.primary: A generated answer grounded in passages retrieved from the reference dataset
outputs.schema_notes: Includes the generated answer plus the specific retrieved passages it drew from, so the pattern is visible to the visitor.

success_criteria: For questions covered by the dataset, the retrieved passages are topically relevant to the question
The generated answer visibly reflects the content of the retrieved passages rather than ignoring them
A visitor unfamiliar with retrieval-augmented generation can follow, from the output, how retrieval fed into the answer

failure_modes.mode: Retrieved passages are irrelevant to the question asked
failure_modes.mitigation: The dataset is kept small and curated so relevant matches are more likely for typical example questions.

failure_modes.mode: The generated answer ignores the retrieved passages entirely
failure_modes.mitigation: The answer is structured to explicitly reference the retrieved content.

failure_modes.mode: Shared generation or embedding capability is unavailable when a question is submitted
failure_modes.mitigation: A clear message is shown indicating the demonstration is temporarily unavailable.

tier_analysis.rationale: The described dataset is explicitly a 'small public dataset,' which is the exact trigger in the rag pattern's when_doesnt list: knowledge that fits in roughly 5,000 tokens and rarely changes should be placed directly in the system prompt and answered with a single structured-output call rather than built out as a full retrieval pipeline. The task itself — turn a natural-language question plus grounding text into a generated answer — is a bounded input/bounded output transformation, squarely matching single_call's when_works criteria, and does not require acting on the world or fetching data outside what's already given.
tier_analysis.compared_to_next_tier_down: The next tier down (embeddings alone) could rank or surface similar passages but cannot generate the natural-language answer the feature requires — embeddings rank and group, they do not write, so single_call's generation capability is necessary here.
borderline_seams: If 'small public dataset' later becomes large, frequently changing, or too big to fit in ~5,000 tokens, this should be re-escalated to rag.
If answers must cite specific retrieved passages for auditability, that requirement would push this back toward the rag tier even at small scale.
risks_of_going_higher: Building embeddings-based retrieval and a retrieval step for a dataset small enough to fit in-prompt adds indexing, chunking, and retrieval-quality engineering with no accuracy benefit.
A full rag pipeline introduces failure modes (irrelevant chunk retrieval, retrieval latency) that a single well-crafted prompt with the whole dataset inline would avoid entirely for this scale.
risks_of_going_lower: Trying to answer via pure deterministic logic (keyword match/lookup) would fail on natural-language questions whose phrasing doesn't match the dataset's exact wording, since meaning rather than surface form drives the answer.
Embeddings alone would only rank/retrieve passages but could not generate the natural-language answer the feature requires.

ai_features.name: custom_text_semantic_placement
ai_features.rough_description: Takes a user-entered custom word, phrase, or sentence and produces its semantic position relative to the curated preset examples in the shared 2D visualization, letting users see how their own text clusters with (or diverges from) existing categories and sentences.
ai_features.purpose: Computes an embedding for user-submitted custom text and projects it into the same fixed 2D semantic space as the curated preset examples, so users can see where their own words semantically fall relative to known categories.

invocation.trigger: User submits custom text in the Embeddings Example App (preset examples are embedded and projected once at build/deploy time, not per-request)

inputs.name: custom_text
inputs.description: User-entered word, phrase, or sentence to be placed on the shared plot

inputs.name: preset_projection_model
inputs.description: Precomputed embedding vectors, fitted 2D projection (e.g. PCA/UMAP transform), and category labels for the curated preset examples; used as the fixed reference space

outputs.primary: The (x, y) coordinate of the custom text within the existing shared 2D plot, computed by embedding the text and applying the same fitted projection used for the presets, plus the custom text's nearest preset neighbors for optional UI highlighting
outputs.schema_notes: { point: { x: number, y: number }, text: string, nearest_neighbors: [{ text, distance }], embedding_model_version: string }. Coordinates must be produced via transform() on the pre-fitted projection model, never a re-fit, so preset positions never move.

success_criteria: Preset examples remain visually clustered by semantic category and do not shift position when custom text is added
Custom text is placed near semantically related presets (validated on a small labeled test set of custom inputs)
Custom text points render as visually distinct markers from preset points
Empty or whitespace-only custom text is rejected before embedding with a clear inline message
Same embedding model and projection pipeline is reused consistently across app sessions and matches the model used elsewhere in the app suite

failure_modes.mode: Projection re-fit on every submission causes preset points to jump around
failure_modes.mitigation: Fit the 2D projection (PCA/UMAP) once on preset embeddings at build time; persist the fitted transform; apply transform-only (no re-fit) to new custom text embeddings

failure_modes.mode: User submits empty or whitespace-only text
failure_modes.mitigation: Client- and server-side validation rejects empty/whitespace input before calling the embedding API, with inline error message

failure_modes.mode: Embedding model differs from the one used for presets or other example apps
failure_modes.mitigation: Pin a single shared embedding model/version in shared_framework_services config; version-tag all stored preset embeddings and validate match at runtime

failure_modes.mode: Custom text is extremely long or contains unsupported characters causing embedding API error
failure_modes.mitigation: Truncate/validate input length client-side; catch API errors and surface a friendly retry message

failure_modes.mode: Out-of-distribution custom text (e.g. gibberish) lands in a misleading/arbitrary spot
failure_modes.mitigation: Document as expected behavior in the educational explanation text; optionally show nearest-neighbor distances so users can judge confidence

ai_features.escalation: On embedding API failure or timeout, show a non-blocking error state in the UI and allow retry; no human review needed since output is a non-critical visualization, not a decision with real-world consequences

eval_approach.offline: Maintain a small labeled test set of custom phrases with expected semantic neighborhoods (e.g. 'kitten' should land near animal presets); verify placement via nearest-neighbor check after each embedding model or projection change
eval_approach.online: Monitor embedding API latency/error rate, rate of empty-input rejections, and spot-check a sample of submitted custom texts' placements weekly
eval_approach.ground_truth: Preset example categories are manually curated and labeled; custom-text placement quality is judged by qualitative nearest-neighbor plausibility rather than strict labels

privacy_safety: Custom text may contain user-entered free text; do not persist beyond the active session/plot state unless explicitly opted into analytics
Do not log raw custom text in long-term logs; if logging is needed for debugging, redact or hash
No content filtering needed for placement itself, but consider basic profanity/PII masking in the displayed label if the plot is shareable

mechanisms.name: structured_outputs
mechanisms.rationale: The projected coordinate and neighbor list must conform to a fixed schema so the frontend can reliably render the point on the shared plot

configuration.schema: { point: {x: number, y: number}, text: string, nearest_neighbors: array, embedding_model_version: string }

served_features.name: Embeddings_Example_App
served_features.purpose: Visually demonstrates the embedding pattern by plotting a curated set of texts in a 2D space based on semantic similarity, letting users add their own text and see it placed among the rest, alongside a short explanation of what embeddings are.

invocation.trigger: A user opens the embeddings example app, or submits custom text within it.

inputs.name: preconfigured_examples
inputs.description: A built-in curated set of words, short phrases, and sentences spanning multiple categories.

inputs.name: custom_text
inputs.description: Text entered by the user to be embedded and placed among the existing examples.

outputs.primary: A 2D visual plot of all texts positioned by semantic similarity, plus an educational explanation of the embedding pattern
outputs.format: Interactive visual plot with distinctly marked custom entries, accompanied by explanatory text
outputs.schema_notes: Each plotted point is labeled with its source text; custom-entered points are visually distinguishable from the preconfigured ones.

success_criteria: Preconfigured examples visibly cluster by semantic category (e.g. animals near animals, emotions near emotions)
Submitting custom text adds it to the same plot, recalculated to include it
Custom text points are clearly visually distinct from preconfigured points
The explanation of the embedding pattern is present and understandable
The app follows the same layout as other example apps and is reachable from the landing page and navigation menu

failure_modes.mode: The plot layout shifts drastically each time custom text is added, making comparison hard
failure_modes.mitigation: Apply the same projection approach consistently across recalculations

failure_modes.mode: Custom text points are not visually distinguishable from preconfigured points
failure_modes.mitigation: Enforce a distinct visual treatment for user-submitted points

failure_modes.mode: This app ends up using a different embedding representation than other apps
failure_modes.mitigation: Require use of the one shared embedding model rather than a separate one
Validate input before attempting to embed and plot it

tier_analysis.rationale: The feature takes free-form, natural-language text (arbitrary user-entered words, phrases, or sentences) and must position it in a semantic space relative to preset examples based on meaning, not exact match or structured fields — this is exactly the 'semantic search / clustering' use case embeddings exist for. A deterministic implementation could not provably place, say, the phrase 'a swift red fox' near 'quick brown fox' or in the correct region relative to curated categories, because that judgment depends on meaning rather than any fixed rule, keyword, or lookup key. No generation is required — the output is a position (coordinates/nearest neighbours in the 2D projection), not written prose, explanation, or summary, so single_call's generation capability is unnecessary and embeddings alone satisfy the requirement.
tier_analysis.compared_to_next_tier_down: Deterministic (e.g., keyword matching against preset categories) would fail on any user input phrased differently from the presets' exact wording, since it can't capture semantic closeness — it would only work for exact or near-exact string matches, defeating the purpose of a semantic map.
risks_of_going_higher: single_call would add unneeded LLM generation cost/latency for what is fundamentally a vector math + projection operation, and could introduce non-determinism in a spatial visualization where users expect consistent placement.
rag or tool_agent would add retrieval/tool machinery with no unstructured document corpus to ground on and no action to take — pure overhead.
risks_of_going_lower: A deterministic (keyword/rule) approach cannot capture semantic similarity for arbitrary user text, so it would misplace synonyms, paraphrases, or novel phrasing relative to the preset examples, undermining the core 'see how your text clusters' value proposition.

ai_features.name: chunking_pipeline
ai_features.rough_description: Enabling infrastructure (chunking pipeline): shared substrate injected because the selected rag feature(s) require it. Not a user-selected feature — foundational and tier-derived.

ai_features.name: embedding_pipeline
ai_features.rough_description: Enabling infrastructure (embedding pipeline): shared substrate injected because the selected rag feature(s) require it. Not a user-selected feature — foundational and tier-derived.

ai_features.name: retriever
ai_features.rough_description: Enabling infrastructure (retriever): shared substrate injected because the selected rag feature(s) require it. Not a user-selected feature — foundational and tier-derived.

ai_features.name: vector_index
ai_features.rough_description: Enabling infrastructure (vector index): shared substrate injected because the selected rag feature(s) require it. Not a user-selected feature — foundational and tier-derived.

provider_strategy.recommendation: This feature requires only a lightweight embeddings-tier model, not a generative/frontier LLM. A compact sentence-embedding model (in the capability class of sentence-transformers' MiniLM/mpnet-sized models, e.g. all-mpnet-base-v2 or comparable ~100-400M parameter embedding models) is sufficient to project custom text into the fixed 2D semantic space, since the task is a deterministic vector projection, not open-ended reasoning or generation. No fallback to a larger/frontier model is warranted for this feature — capability needs are flat and low, and the structured_outputs mechanism here only constrains the embedding/coordinate output shape, not reasoning quality. If the embedding model changes over time, the 2D projection space must be recomputed/recalibrated consistently, since embedding-space compatibility (not raw model 'power') is the binding constraint.
provider_strategy.rationale: The sole AI feature in this project is an embeddings-only transformation (text -> vector -> 2D coordinate), which does not require the general reasoning, instruction-following, or generative capability that justifies mid-tier or frontier LLMs. Sizing the capability tier to the actual task avoids over-provisioning power (and the cost/latency that comes with it) for a fixed, low-complexity embedding operation, while leaving concrete provider/model selection to the downstream stack-selection phase.

prompt_versioning.recommendation: Store the rag_example_app's prompt template (including the structured-output schema/instructions) as a versioned artifact (e.g., a file with semantic version or content hash) checked into the same repo as the retrieval and app code, rather than inline in code. Pin the exact prompt version used at each generation call in logs/traces alongside the retrieved context and model output, so answers can be reproduced or rolled back if a schema or grounding regression appears after a prompt edit.
prompt_versioning.rationale: Because this is a single-feature project built around structured_outputs, the main versioning risk is silent drift between the prompt's schema instructions and the actual output parser/validator. Explicit version pinning and logging let the team detect and roll back a prompt change that breaks the structured-output contract or degrades grounding quality, even with just one feature in scope.

nfr_goals: All example apps present a consistent, unified look and navigation experience
The platform operates using only free-tier language, embedding, and search resources
New example apps can be added without disrupting existing ones
Interactions within example apps feel responsive enough for live demonstration
The system degrades gracefully and communicates clearly when a free-tier usage limit is reached
